ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**1:** Both sections argue that over-relying on one monolithic prompt produces an unreliable, hard-to-debug system. The generated section's personal anecdote (a document-summary/entity-extraction/FAQ/JSON mega-prompt that produced 'a mess of inconsistent outputs, high latency, and a debugging nightmare') conveys the same substance as the expected section's 'black box' framing through a different narrative device. The opening Lessons 1-4 callback is a brief, proportionate addition.

The Challenge with Complex Single LLM Calls:
**1:** Both sections argue single complex prompts are hard to debug, lack modularity, suffer from lost-in-the-middle, and are token-inefficient, and both walk through the identical FAQ example ending in a single-vs-multi-source citation/hallucination risk. As in the previously graded articles, the expected section's phrasing-sensitivity/reproducibility point and its context-overflow/truncation point have no clean standalone counterpart -- this section's token-efficiency discussion is about model-cost trade-offs and multi-problem format brittleness, not context truncation specifically. Given the central thesis and most supporting mechanisms are present, this is treated as tolerable compression, consistent with the other articles graded so far.

The Power of Modularity: Why Chain LLM Calls?:
**1:** This is the most complete match of this specific section found so far: all five of the guideline's/expected section's benefit concepts are present (modularity, accuracy, debugging, and flexibility explicitly paired with optimization via the cheap/expensive-model example), and three of the four trade-off points are explicit and distinct -- including, for the first time across the articles graded, a clearly separate 'instructions may lose their meaning when split' point alongside (not merged with) the information-loss/context-degradation point. Only the 'glue code'/maintenance-burden downside has no counterpart.

Building a Sequential Workflow: FAQ Generation Pipeline:
**1:** Both sections build the identical 3-step chain, combine it into a sequential_workflow function, measure the same 22.20-second execution time, and reach the same conclusion about the reliability/speed trade-off. The added real-world case-study reference (AppFolio, Athena Intelligence, LangGraph) is a proportionate, on-topic addition that does not displace any expected idea.

Optimizing Sequential Workflows With Parallel Processing:
**1:** Both sections explain the independence of answering/sourcing, build the same async function pair and asyncio.gather-based parallel_workflow, and report the same 22.20s-to-8.98s speedup. The rate-limit guidance here is the most thorough version found across the articles graded so far -- covering backoff, jitter, thundering-herd avoidance, retry budgets, and circuit breakers -- which, while using two different specific techniques than the expected section's four (Retry-After headers and client-side queueing are not mentioned; retry budgets and circuit breakers are added instead), matches the expected section's overall level of detail rather than compressing it.

Introducing Dynamic Behavior: Routing and Conditional Logic:
**1:** The core ideas -- fixed workflows can't adapt, an LLM call can act as the classifier, this follows divide-and-conquer, and a customer-service illustration -- are all present. The expected section's model-routing callout is satisfied by this section's 'cost-aware routing that sends a query to a more powerful model only when a cheaper one returns a low-confidence score' point. Beyond this, the section adds substantial, well-sourced depth not present in the expected section: a survey of routing techniques (rule-based, semantic, cost-aware, fine-tuned classifiers), a production cascade-routing architecture, and a decision-theory framing (allow/abstain/deny based on confidence thresholds) -- see DepthEnhancement and BreadthEnhancement below for the detailed instance analysis.

Building a Basic Routing Workflow:
**0:** Both sections implement the identical IntentEnum/UserIntent classification model, the same classify_intent function, the same three specialized prompts, and the same handle_query router. As with every other article graded so far, the expected section's paragraph on intent-classification best practices (taxonomy design, high-quality examples for edge cases, a two-stage retrieve-then-classify architecture) has no counterpart -- this section's own addition (combining intent and complexity/depth into a single classification call) is a genuinely new, well-sourced idea, but it is not a substitute for the specific missing content, so CoreContent still fails on that missing idea cluster.

Orchestrator-Worker Pattern: Dynamic Task Decomposition:
**0:** Both sections define the orchestrator-worker pattern the same way and frame its flexibility advantage over parallelization identically, and both walk through the same three-issue customer query with matching Task/QueryTypeEnum schemas, workers, synthesizer, and main pipeline function, all shown in full working code (unlike one of the other articles graded, where this code was heavily abbreviated). However, as with every other article graded so far, the expected section's paragraph on the pattern's implementation challenges (bottleneck risk, incomplete decomposition, synthesis/conflict-resolution difficulty) has no counterpart. The operating-system-scheduler analogy added in its place is a genuinely valuable, well-sourced addition (see BreadthEnhancement below), but it illustrates a different point (a decentralized-vs-centralized architectural contrast) rather than covering the expected section's specific risks, so CoreContent still fails on that missing idea cluster.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections recap the same four patterns, and this version pairs each with essentially the same benefit as the expected section (chaining=modularity/debugging, parallelization=latency, routing=specialized handling, orchestrator-worker=flexible decomposition), just in prose rather than a list. Both close by connecting the lesson to the wider practice of AI engineering and previewing what comes next. The next-lesson preview covers the same theme as the expected section (tools/function calling) without citing a specific lesson number, which -- per established precedent -- is a guideline_adherence matter rather than a CoreContent one.
